articles.title: A Golden Chapter at Sivagangai – A Farewell Note
articles.shortDescription: A Golden Chapter at Sivagangai – A Farewell Note
articles.longDescription:
Our time at Sivagangai was nothing short of a wonderful experience. We spent 25 memorable months there, from 22nd May 2023 until 27th June 2025, during which Asha served as the District Collector. It was not just a place of stay—it became our extended home, filled with warmth, affection, and unforgettable bonds.


From the very beginning, we were embraced by the love and hospitality of the people of Sivagangai, especially the incredible staff at the Camp Office—both inside and outside the residence. It truly felt like an extended family, with a rich blend of cultures, habits, and emotions. For me and Jayasree, it was as though we gained many sons and daughters during our stay.


Priyatharsini, the team leader of the Camp Office, was our pillar. A dynamic, committed, and highly capable individual, she led the team with unmatched energy and grace. Her discipline, sharp mind, and dedication ensured both the official and residential spaces functioned smoothly. Her care extended beyond duty—she tracked my safety and wellbeing even during my short trips with the concern of a family member. Her family became part of our daily conversations, and we were deeply involved in her daughters’ education, just as we were with our granddaughter Padma. She even arranged regular health check-ups for me, always thoughtful about my well-being.


Balamurugan was the quiet powerhouse behind the seamless running of the house. He had an uncanny ability to spot and resolve every little issue without needing instruction. His day would begin at 6 a.m., preparing a special black tea for me made with palm jaggery, clove, ginger, and cardamom. Breakfast would be ready by 8:30 a.m., and he would ensure Padma’s school bag, shoes, socks, water bottle, and lunch were all perfectly arranged. His energy and work ethic were phenomenal—like an eagle spotting its prey, he identified work before anyone else noticed. He was an immense support to Jayasree.


Subhadra, our cheerful cook, shared a beautiful bond with Padma. They were like friends, spending their evenings together after school. Alongside cooking, Subhadra joined Jayasree and Padma for farm visits, enjoying the harvest and bonding with the goats.


Amutharaj (Amudan) was another of Padma’s close companions. A natural comedian with Vadivelu-style humour, he shared endless light-hearted banter with Padma. She became his tutor in English, Malayalam, music, dance, and more, while he taught her Tamil. A multi-talented soul, Amudan was also a creative mind—crafting school models and DIY projects with flair.


Kaleeswaran, another of Padma’s "students," always brightened her days with his friendly presence.


Veeran, officially the cleaner, was much more—a silent, sincere boy who became a dear family member and a friend to Padma.


Thankaraj and Suresh, who managed the farm, established a warm relationship with us. Suresh, whom Padma fondly called “Sureshannae,” was especially close to her, just like Subhadra.


The dhobi Aashirvadam and wife Bhanu were devout and dutiful, always meticulous with their work.


Muthuraman, one of our drivers, called me Appa like many others. Jayasree would often say, even our own son Sreekuttan doesn't call me in such a soft tone! Ravi, though he left after an accident, and Jayakumar, who served earlier, were also excellent drivers. Jayakumar’s daughters, Ananya and Dhananya, visited us and became good friends with Padma.


Prabhu, Asha’s personal assistant, was a smart and efficient coordinator who handled responsibilities diligently. Ramesh and others too ensured all our needs were met without us even having to ask.


Murugesan, the Collector’s vehicle driver, was more than just a driver—he showed a touching concern for Asha’s daily routine. Sebastian, soft-spoken and kind, also stood out for his caring nature.


In the office, Sreeni, Murugan, and Rajasekharan left lasting impressions with their friendly and committed work.Gunman Vicky, Suresh and others were so close as family members and friends to Padma.Although Alagu was transferred early on, he continued to maintain the relationship even after the transfer.


The person who cleaned the campus, lovingly addressed as "Ayya", worked quietly and devotedly, almost like a saint. His dedication and humility are rare in today’s world.


Even the sentries at the main gate, who changed every day, left fond memories in our hearts.


Other regular visitors included Sumitra, the dance teacher and her family, and the tailor, Mahalekshmi ,all of whom contributed to the warm, homely atmosphere.


And then, there was Padmavathi, the little spark in our lives, who thoroughly enjoyed every moment at the Camp Office. Her bonds with everyone—from the cooks to the drivers—were special and genuine.


Our son, Sreekuttan, currently working in Ramanathapuram, would visit us during holidays. The staff eagerly awaited his visits—he was a natural entertainer, involving everyone in cooking, sports, music, and dance. Though young, he was lovingly called “Annan” by all.


Sub Collector Ayush was like a son to us — a regular visitor to our home who shared many joyful moments, often playing with Padma. We truly miss him too.


Asha got a parent warmth from Justice.M.Chockalingam and A.R.P.Murugesan needs special mention.They considered Padma as their granddaughter and she also had such a warmth sharing the time with them and the hospitality.


The love and affection Padma received at Oxford school also need special mention.The founder of the school Syamala Venkatesan, teachers Pramila,Suba Pavitra,Nisha and staff members made her days at Oxford happy and prosperous


I might have missed names,but all people involved in many ways remain in our heart with colours and sorry if anybody left mentioned.


In total, these two years at Sivagangai will remain a golden period in our lives. We leave with hearts full of gratitude and memories etched deep in our souls.


Farewell, Sivagangai! Thank you for gifting us such a beautiful chapter in our life journey 💛

articles.title: Freedom  -  Part   one
articles.shortDescription:
Freedom is a subject that has been explored in many ways by philosophers across time. But what truly is freedom?
According to Osho, true freedom lies in the ability to say yes, say no, or remain silent—whenever it is necessary. One who can do this is truly free.
articles.longDescription:
When Osho speaks about freedom, he highlights two simple yet powerful words: yes and no. According to him, true freedom lies in the ability to say yes, say no, or remain silent—whenever and however one chooses.


Reading that, I was reminded that yes and no are arguably the two most powerful words in the English language. Interestingly, there is no single-word equivalent for them in Malayalam. I am not sure whether any other language has such precise substitutes either. In Malayalam, yes and no can take on many shades of meaning, and often, a variety of words must be used in their place. This could be seen as a limitation of the language—or perhaps a reflection of cultural nuance.


Yet, Osho’s idea of freedom is, in many ways, only relative. The deeper reality is that nothing in the universe is truly free. Does saying yes, no, or choosing silence truly make one free?


Consider nature: a flowing river, the wind in motion, the vast ocean, or a mountain standing tall—all appear free, yet none are without limitations. Even animals and birds have invisible boundaries. But it is humans who perhaps experience these constraints the most.


Even Osho himself, with all his philosophical insight, was not free from the comforts and dependencies he embraced. When the body is held hostage by hunger, thirst, desire, and greed, how can the soul—or the energy within—experience freedom? Even when this soul escapes the body at the time of death, it does not attain pure independence. That energy still yearns to bind itself again, to enter into something, somewhere.


In essence, the ultimate truth may be this: no one truly desires absolute freedom. And even if they do, they are unlikely to attain it.


(To be continued…)

articles.title: Freedom-part 2--Do humans truly love freedom?
articles.shortDescription:
Do humans truly love freedom?
It's a profound question. Throughout history, humanity has fought to end slavery and oppression — yet many still willingly submit to the chains of caste, religion, and political ideologies. While the human story is, in part, a struggle for liberation, there's also a deep-rooted psychological — perhaps even genetic — tendency in many to seek belonging over freedom. This often manifests as a kind of voluntary servitude. People can become addicted to identity, tradition, and dogma, even when these cause suffering. In many cases, it seems that comfort in the familiar outweighs the desire to be truly free.
articles.longDescription:
When we talk about freedom, we find that it exists on many levels. There are both visible and invisible forms of unfreedom. Domestic animals live with clear restrictions: a bird is confined to its cage, cattle are tethered by a rope, and a dog’s boundaries are set by its owner’s home or field. Even stray dogs, though uncaged, live within the social limits imposed by themselves or human environments. Wild animals, while seemingly free, are still limited by territory and survival needs. Yet, their physical freedom far surpasses that of domesticated animals.


Primitive humans likely experienced this kind of physical freedom in abundance. Perhaps it is due to this genetic memory that modern humans still crave greater freedom.


Over time, those who once roamed freely began forming tribes. In conflicts, the defeated were often enslaved by the victors. Harsh rulers chained the weak, stripping them of physical freedom and selling them like commodities. Slavery, once enforced with iron chains, gradually evolved into more subtle systems. The landlord-tenant model replaced open slavery. Large landowners gave landless people shelter, only to bind them with poverty and dependency. They were denied education, keeping them permanently subservient.


Religion, once introduced, added further layers to these chains. Hierarchies were codified: some declared themselves superior and relegated others to lower castes, entrenching a form of social slavery that persisted for centuries.


With the rise of democracy, some progress was made. However, it has not been absolute. The changes that occurred in Kerala, for instance, have not been mirrored across all of India. In many villages today, caste divisions still prevail. Hindu society remains split into upper castes, backward castes, Scheduled Castes, and Scheduled Tribes. For many, this division results in a deep lack of freedom that persists even today.


Despite the efforts of social reformers—who tried to dismantle these mental chains—the caste-based mindset remains unresolved. Even temples, believed to be the abode of God, uphold this social hierarchy.


All systems of governance, in one way or another, echo the master-slave dynamic. Even democracies, built on the idea of equality, reproduce these patterns. Within political movements, a similar hierarchy exists: central leaders take the place of upper castes, followed by state, district, taluk, and village-level leaders. The masses at the bottom become tools—used by those in power in exchange for minor benefits and freebies.


It is often said that humans are thinking beings. But in truth, many are not. The majority are trapped by the addictions of caste, religion, and politics—and they do not wish to escape. Just as people knowingly continue to use alcohol, tobacco, or drugs despite understanding the harm, so too do they cling to social constructs that limit their freedom.


This is the paradox: even when the chains are invisible, people are reluctant to break free. (To be continued)

articles.title: Freedom -part-3- Unfreedom and religion
articles.shortDescription:
Freedom – Part 3: Unfreedom and  Religion

The most significant trap a human being faces on Earth is religion. Though God is a man-made concept, it has overshadowed humanity and created deep divisions—separating people on every front in the name of faith. To live truly and peacefully on this Earth, one must break free from this trap and seek the truth through their own understanding.
articles.longDescription:
Religion is the first chain that binds human freedom. It is implanted in children at a very young age. The earliest lesson in discrimination is often this: the difference between my religion and yours. In India, this division is most commonly seen between those who go to temples and those who go to mosques or churches.


What children should be taught is this: the Hindu calls it "God", the Christian says "Jehovah", and the Muslim says "Allah". But what they are referring to is essentially the same—a formless, universal force. They should be led to understand that this divine presence is the universe at the macroscopic level and the cell at the microscopic level. That is pure science.


Instead, children are taught to worship idols or prophets. Even though language—words and sentences—is a human creation, we ascribe divine status to them. In this way, religion imparts an unscientific and dogmatic worldview from childhood, shaping minds to be limited and imperfect. As a result, people grow up flawed, live within constraints, and die never having broken free of them.


Parents, even those who know deep down that there is no separate god outside the universe, still teach their children otherwise. They instill the idea of heaven and hell, despite having no evidence or direct experience of either. This act—teaching others what one does not truly know—is the very foundation on which religion thrives.


So, what is religion? Who needs it?


What we really need is to teach one another how to live this human life with mutual love, joy, and responsibility. But most people are not ready for that. And even those who are, often end up isolated. In truth, every child born on this earth is at risk of being trapped by religion. And generation after generation, people unknowingly pass on this mindset to the next.


Instead of urging children to observe, question, and discover truth on their own, we tell them: Don’t think—this is the truth. Follow this path—my path. And so, the journey that the child embarks on is lined with fear and uncertainty. We cut him off from the true source of mental freedom—as if severing him from his mother’s umbilical cord only to bind him again, this time with chains of belief.


An ordinary human being first needs physical freedom, and then seeks mental freedom. If he goes further, he might strive for spiritual freedom—a path far more difficult, and not essential for everyone. Even among ascetics, very few achieve true spiritual freedom. Many spiritual leaders end their lives still entangled in worldly desires, both of the body and the mind. So can we really say they attained spiritual perfection?


True spiritual life belongs only to those rare souls who, having transcended emotional and mental life, renounce everything and return to the forest. These individuals are no longer reformers or leaders; they are solitary seekers. In contrast, those who lead religious institutions or movements often remain bound to the emotional stage of life. They don’t even attain mental freedom. Even ascetics who become social reformers, though they bring great changes to society, often do not attain spiritual freedom. They die burdened by the concerns of the movement they started or the ashram they built.


To truly live a spiritual life, one must walk away from it all—not just physically, but mentally. They must return to nature, to simplicity, to solitude. And how many truly do that?


In the end, those who attain spiritual freedom are souls who die without leaving a mark. Their deaths are not celebrated. They disappear quietly, without followers or monuments. (To be continued)

articles.title: Freedom – Part 4: Protection and Conflict
articles.shortDescription: Conflict is a fundamental force of human life. It operates continuously within the individual—internally and subtly—and this internal struggle reflects on a global, even cosmic, scale. The same conflict that occurs in the human psyche can be seen magnified in the world around us. The Earth itself experiences conflict—in the form of earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis. The same dynamic plays out across the solar system, the Milky Way, and the entire universe.
articles.longDescription:
The various levels of human slavery are intriguing—particularly the kind that individuals willingly impose upon themselves for the sake of material comfort. Among these, the protection offered by religion and caste stands out as especially significant. When a person chooses to live under the shadow of the caste and religion inherited from their parents, they are, in effect, submitting to a system that offers security in the material world. In doing so, they become a slave to that system.


This tendency extends beyond religion and caste. Individuals often become part of organizations or political movements, seeking protection during their education or employment. The sense of material security that these affiliations provide drives them to comply. Even the family is a structure built around the fulfillment of physical needs, offering shelter and emotional support. Friendships, too, function within this same framework of material and emotional convenience.


In essence, modern slavery lies in the way a person, as part of a group, surrenders himself to material desires. What is striking is that most people have no real desire to break free from this form of bondage.


Even when someone transitions from one group to another due to inner turmoil or dissatisfaction, they often find themselves entangled in yet another collective. This new group, too, brings its own share of discomforts and disagreements. People move forward within such systems—sometimes by confronting what they dislike, and at other times by compromising. This cycle is driven by a deep-rooted slave mentality that has been passed down through generations. It's like the dynamic between iron and a magnet—pushing and pulling, separating and reuniting.


This is why personal conflicts are common—within homes, political movements, and organizations. Most individuals navigate life by managing these struggles—either through confrontation or adjustment. The extraordinary mental strength required to live independently, outside these systems, is rare.


Conflict exists at every boundary. More importantly, it also exists within. A nation comprises people of different beliefs, cultures, languages, and ethnicities—leading to both personal and ideological clashes. Conflict is just as prevalent within families. Yet, despite all these frictions, people unite when it comes to shared interests—whether for the sake of the family, the nation, or alliances between like-minded countries. Thus, harmony and conflict constantly alternate, like ebb and flow.


Ultimately, conflict is a fundamental force of human life. It operates continuously within the individual—internally and subtly—and this internal struggle reflects on a global, even cosmic, scale. The same conflict that occurs in the human psyche can be seen magnified in the world around us. The Earth itself experiences conflict—in the form of earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis. The same dynamic plays out across the solar system, the Milky Way, and the entire universe. (To be continued...)

articles.title: The Jamaat case quashed by  the Delhi High Court is a striking example of how urgently our systems need reform.
articles.shortDescription: Reforming our legal and policing systems is not an option — it is an urgent necessity if we wish to build a truly just and developed India.
articles.longDescription:
Five years ago, in the early days of COVID-19, a Tablighi Jamaat congregation was held in Delhi. Following this, the police registered 16 FIRs against 70 Indian citizens for allegedly hosting foreign delegates who attended the gathering, accusing them of violating lockdown orders and health protocols. According to the law, such cases should be investigated swiftly and either taken to trial or closed within a reasonable timeframe — ideally within weeks. Instead, this matter dragged on for five years with no resolution or progress. Finally, on July 16, 2025, the Delhi High Court quashed the charges, bringing an end to years of uncertainty for the accused.


This case raises several critical questions about our justice system:


*Is there no binding time limit for an FIR to be investigated and filed in court? *If an FIR is found to be baseless or wrongly filed, shouldn’t it be withdrawn immediately? *Shouldn’t those falsely implicated receive an official apology and appropriate compensation for the mental agony and reputational damage suffered? *Shouldn’t the officials responsible for such misuse of power and violation of human rights face accountability?


As we dream of becoming a developed nation by 2047, we must ask ourselves: will our justice system continue to remain stuck in this state of delay, inefficiency, and injustice? Or will it become even more unaccountable and oppressive if we do not act now?


Reforming our legal and policing systems is not an option — it is an urgent necessity if we wish to build a truly just and developed India.

articles.title: Eight cities in Kerala are among the top hundred cleanest cities in India
articles.shortDescription: Eight of the top 100 cleanest cities in the Union Ministry of Urban Affairs’ Swachh Survekshan ranking are from Kerala. The commendable efforts made under the leadership of M.B. Rajesh, the Minister for Local Self-Government, deserve special appreciation for this achievement.
articles.longDescription:
It is indeed a matter of pride that eight of the top 100 cleanest cities in the Union Ministry of Urban Affairs’ Swachh Survekshan ranking are from Kerala. The commendable efforts made under the leadership of M.B. Rajesh, the Minister for Local Self-Government, deserve special appreciation for this achievement.


The survey has ranked Mattanur in Kannur as the cleanest city in Kerala. Cities like Guruvayur, Alappuzha, Thiruvananthapuram, Kozhikode, Kollam, Thrissur and Kochi have also secured places in the top 100 list. The dedicated efforts of the officials, municipal authorities, and the countless workers who toiled sincerely at the grassroots level deserve wholehearted praise.


Kerala, with its high population density, continues to face the serious challenge of waste management. While it is heartening that eight of our cities have risen from a past of littered riversides and unclean surroundings to national recognition, many more towns and villages still have a long way to go.


One worrying trend is the growing habit among Malayalis of relying on store-bought cooked food, which is resulting in increased plastic waste. This can be tackled only through greater public awareness and a change in attitudes.


Recognising that tourism is one of our main sources of income, Kerala must strive to emulate cities like Indore — which has consistently topped the cleanliness rankings — by allocating more funds in the budget and ensuring robust public participation in waste management initiatives.


Let us hope we continue on this path with renewed resolve and collective responsibility.

articles.title: Power, Corruption, and the Weakness of Democracy
articles.shortDescription: In a democracy, deficiencies in the legal system and judiciary can create avenues for the powerful to avoid facing justice
articles.longDescription:
Democracy is undoubtedly the best system of governance, but the protection it often extends to criminals, murderers, corrupt politicians, the wealthy, and the unscrupulous tarnishes its glory. Democracy can only be truly beautiful when it brings together the best features of all good systems in the world. The greatest weakness of democracy lies in its flawed legal system


Under dictatorships or monarchies, the legal machinery often acts swiftly and decisively, supported by strict laws that instill genuine fear of punishment. In democracies, however, the law is frequently undermined and treated with contempt by those who know how to manipulate it.


I say this today because of the glaring example of the corruption cases involving former Bihar Chief Minister and Union Railway Minister Lalu Prasad Yadav. The infamous fodder scam of the 1990s, the IRCTC scam between 2004 and 2009, the land-for-jobs scam, and allegations of massive benami properties together amount to scams worth hundreds of crores of rupees. Yet, a person facing such grave charges is out on bail on health grounds, remains politically active, and continues to evade justice while endless investigations drag on aimlessly.


This sorry state of affairs exposes the cracks in our legal system. Even in the ‘developed India’ we dream of for 2047, cases like these may still linger unresolved, reminding us that sometimes all we can do is stand by and watch—powerless to see the rule of law prevail.

articles.title: The history of Kerala CPM will have to be recorded as before and after V.S.
articles.shortDescription: V.S. Achuthanandan passed away at the age of one hundred and two, fulfilling the fullness of a human life. V.S., who led a tireless and restless life until the age of ninety-five, had been resting for the past six years. He left us yesterday. We see V.S. as the last leader in the EMS and Nayanar tradition — leaders who believed that at least some Marxian ideals could be practically implemented and who genuinely worked for it. V.S. was a leader who followed Maoist approaches, giving prime importance to farmers, workers, and land reforms. He was a strict leader who took an uncompromising stand against corruption — a staunch communist who never wavered from his beliefs.
articles.longDescription:
V.S. Achuthanandan passed away at the age of one hundred and two, fulfilling the fullness of a human life. V.S., who led a tireless and restless life until the age of ninety-five, had been resting for the past six years. He left us yesterday. We see V.S. as the last leader in the EMS and Nayanar tradition — leaders who believed that at least some Marxian ideals could be practically implemented and who genuinely worked for it. V.S. was a leader who followed Maoist approaches, giving prime importance to farmers, workers, and land reforms. He was a strict leader who took an uncompromising stand against corruption — a staunch communist who never wavered from his beliefs.


Yet, like many communist leaders, he too faced rejection from within the party. With the advent of globalization and privatization, the communist movement in India transformed significantly. The party leadership gradually came into the hands of millennial Marxists — a new generation that began prioritizing the needs and interests of the middle class and the affluent. In these times, when people at all levels of the party seem to chase wealth and power, we can clearly divide the history of the party into two phases: before and after V.S.


When I worked at Kerala House and the Malayalam Mission, I spoke to V.S. only on official matters. His style was to listen intently and reply in a few measured words. I still remember that there was factionalism among the staff at Kerala House — only those considered V.S.’s supporters could freely access his room.


In 1996, after the Politburo meeting that followed V.S.’s defeat in Mararikulam — despite the Left Front securing a clear majority — a historic discussion took place. On the morning before leaving for the airport, E.K. Nayanar, Pinarayi Vijayan, and V.S. sat together in room number 101 of Kerala House for a secret meeting. I remember Vijaya Mohan of Malayala Manorama and I discussed what might have transpired there. None of us imagined that it was the meeting where they decided not to make Susheela Gopalan the Chief Minister, and instead Nayanar — who hadn’t even contested — would take charge. Politics can create unexpected miracles. Such miracles include V.S. becoming Chief Minister at the age of eighty-two, Pinarayi stepping into that role later, and the continuation of that administration.


Although many labelled V.S. as regressive for giving priority to the environment over certain development activities, it is noteworthy that several key developmental initiatives were undertaken during his tenure as Chief Minister. He never hesitated to act when convinced of what was right. History has marked many instances where V.S. displayed extraordinary conviction — from his fight against corruption to his progressive stance on women’s issues.


No one is perfect, not even V.S. But we bid farewell to the beauty of that imperfection.

articles.title: When Justice Sleeps: The Unsettling Legacy of  Mumbai Bombing and Malegaon Cases
articles.shortDescription: If justice continues to falter in  grave cases, the nation risks losing more than just legal credibility — it erodes public faith in the very idea of accountability. The Justice is delayed , denied and ultimately disrespected .
articles.longDescription:
The long-drawn trials in the Malegaon 2008 blast and the 2006 Mumbai train bombings have exposed deep cracks in India’s criminal justice system. While hundreds lost their lives or limbs, and families waited for closure, what they received instead were hostile witnesses, changing investigative narratives, and endless procedural delays.


The acquittals, bail grants, and judicial leniency shown to prime accused — some now sitting in public office — raise troubling questions. Were the initial charges weak, the evidence fabricated, or the system simply unwilling to carry cases to a just conclusion?


When the police fail to investigate with integrity, and courts hesitate to convict where evidence once seemed strong, justice itself becomes the casualty. The signal sent is dangerous: that even terror cases can be politicized, manipulated, or quietly buried under paperwork and time.


If justice continues to falter in such grave cases, the nation risks losing more than just legal credibility — it erodes public faith in the very idea of accountability. Here, the Justice is delayed , denied and ultimately disrespected .

articles.title: Rethinking Vacations and Exams in Kerala Schools
articles.shortDescription: There is a serious discussion in Kerala about replacing the traditional summer vacation with a monsoon vacation. This is my opinion on the changes that have already been discussed at various levels
articles.longDescription:
An idea recently put forward by Kerala Education Minister V. Sivankutty has sparked much discussion. The core of the debate is whether the traditional midsummer vacation should be replaced with a monsoon vacation. While many who prefer conventional methods opposed this change, those who welcome innovation supported it. I too stand with those who favor change. Since the real impact of such a reform can be known only after implementation, the practical approach is to try it out, even if there is initial resistance.


A notable suggestion came from Kanthapuram, who proposed combining the scorching month of May with the devastating monsoon of June to form a single vacation. He also suggested reducing the number of examinations from three to two. Both are valuable ideas. I would like to extend this thought further with a slightly modified proposal.


If the end-of-year examination is deemed necessary, it should be conducted by the beginning of March, with results published before the end of that month. The new academic year should start on April 1 and continue until April 30. Then, from May 1 to June 30, students can enjoy a combined summer–monsoon vacation. Classes can resume on July 1.


Examinations should also move beyond the outdated practice of testing mere memory. Instead of Onam, Christmas, and annual exams, logical assessments based on the lessons taught each month should be conducted. The average of these scores can determine a child’s progress. If two major exams are considered unavoidable, they should be designed with logical, open-book questions rather than rote-based ones. The goal must be to develop a child’s ability to analyze and apply knowledge, not just memorize and reproduce it.


A balanced grading system could be created by combining the scores from monthly exams, a half-yearly exam, and the annual exam. At the same time, there should be a transparent mechanism to review complaints regarding marks in both monthly and annual assessments. For this transformation to succeed, teachers must be adequately empowered and trained. Steps to strengthen and equip them should go hand-in-hand with academic reforms.

articles.title: Freedom - chapter 5
articles.shortDescription: Man’s greatest strength lies in his ability to change. He adapts to both happiness and sorrow, even when they confront him relentlessly. He swallows bitter medicine with the same ease with which he tastes sweetness. Just as a rose has thorns, night follows day, and summer gives way to autumn, joy and sorrow travel together. The human body itself is a collection of positive and negative cells. The same pattern extends to the family, society, country, world, and universe. All these are chains—each one linked to another. These chains bind not only humans but all living beings. The reason this is less visible among animals is the limitation of their brains. Whether that limitation is a strength or a weakness is something science still needs to discover.
articles.longDescription:
Freedom and Its Chains: Reflections on the Individual, Family, and Society

Man’s greatest strength lies in his ability to change. He adapts to both happiness and sorrow, even when they confront him relentlessly. He swallows bitter medicine with the same ease with which he tastes sweetness. Just as a rose has thorns, night follows day, and summer gives way to autumn, joy and sorrow travel together. The human body itself is a collection of positive and negative cells. The same pattern extends to the family, society, country, world, and universe. All these are chains—each one linked to another. These chains bind not only humans but all living beings. The reason this is less visible among animals is the limitation of their brains. Whether that limitation is a strength or a weakness is something science still needs to discover.


It is often said that man comes to earth crying and leaves making others cry. It is true that when a person dies, someone mourns. But we cannot say whether the person who dies in a sudden accident or in sleep has time to cry. Those who die in pain may cry, but death itself is an undeniable reality. No matter how wicked a person may have been, there will always be someone who weeps for them. Birds and animals are also mourned when they die. Even plants, when they wither, might evoke silent grief in the surrounding vegetation. Natural disasters and cosmic changes also carry their own form of lament. Life, therefore, is a wonder—not only to humans but to the universe itself.


The difference between humans and animals lies in the laws that govern their existence. Animals too have laws, but these are unwritten patterns of nature. Man, however, has gone beyond them. He rewrites the laws given by nature and places himself outside the general animal community. Modern humans—descendants of primitive ancestors—are changing every day. They create new laws, constitutions, and systems of governance to maintain power. Those who attempt to break free from these cages are punished or threatened. Society dictates how one must live and defines what is right and wrong. Systems of enforcement ensure these laws are followed. Over time, laws are rewritten and constitutions amended to suit the interests of rulers. Ordinary people either support or oppose these changes depending on the communities or groups they belong to. Those who resist may protest for a while, but eventually, most accept the chains and even wear them like ornaments.


Anyone who dares to defy the system and strive for absolute freedom risks losing both body and mind. Power crushes such individuals, often driving them to death—releasing only their souls. How many truly wish to be free of these chains? Despite the suffering that exists between birth and death, humans cling to life and wish to prolong it. Very few are exceptions. Life is a rare gift from the universe, and to experience it—even with its lack of complete freedom—should be considered the ultimate goal and duty of existence.


Every person is responsible for their own life. We may choose to live in submission, but it is up to us to decide what we submit to. Some submit to their family, sacrificing personal desires for the sake of loved ones. Others live for society, prioritizing social welfare over individual or family pleasures. Some dedicate themselves to their country, scientific progress, or other higher causes. Yet, there are those who submit only to themselves. For them, personal happiness, health, and interests are paramount. Family, society, and friendship mean little beyond entertainment. Though they may justify their choices with arguments of freedom, their lives are ultimately selfish. Only a small minority among them move toward true spirituality; the rest simply escape responsibility. Such evasion is not freedom—it is a step below humanity. Life is a challenge, and running away from it is cowardice. Those who refuse to face challenges stagnate intellectually, seeking refuge in fate or God during crises, only to find no real peace.


What, then, is family? Why does it exist? Some philosophers claim that individuals are fundamentally isolated, and that parents, spouses, friends, and children encountered between birth and death are mere illusions. But this view is flawed. No child can become a useful member of society without the care and love of parents—or at least one of them. When other relatives or institutions raise children, many struggle with emotional or psychological issues, and those who escape such effects are rare.


The husband–wife relationship, however, is different. Often it carries the dynamics of master and slave, or at the very least, a sense of submission. The primary goal of marriage, whether arranged by families or chosen through love, is mating and procreation, like all other living beings. Various factors influence the attraction between man and woman, but discomfort within marriage is natural—it is only the degree that varies. Peace exists only when responsibilities are shared equally and mutual respect is maintained, with personal spaces carefully protected.


Unfortunately, in many marriages, one partner subjugates the other—mentally, physically, or emotionally. In such cases, the submissive partner becomes the slave, while the dominant plays the master. In more developed societies, such marriages often break apart. When conflicts intensify after marriage and children are born, many couples make compromises for the sake of their children. Here, the one who compromises is not weak but strong. The problematic partner continues a selfish life, sometimes using emotional manipulation, including threats of suicide, while staying mentally and physically detached. They may pretend to care for the children, but their love and responsibility are often superficial.


Marriage, therefore, is an uncomfortable system. Yet it is this very system that sustains society, builds nations, and gives birth to the next generation. Family is a unique structure where sweetness and bitterness coexist. Love and lust, in this context, can sometimes feel like the greatest deceptions of life. Those who have endured the trials of marriage often warn the younger generation not to fall into the same trap—but new relationships still bloom, as though each person must experience the fire for themselves. Most people, like moths drawn to a flame, are destined to repeat the cycle.

articles.title: Freedom – Part Six
articles.shortDescription:
Osho once said that no one truly wants to take responsibility; everyone simply wants freedom.
If that were completely true, the systems we see today—let alone Osho’s own commune—would never have existed.
Society functions and progresses only because there are enough people, in every sphere from family to government, who are willing to sacrifice their personal freedom and endure hardship.
If every individual were to become absolutely free, all existing systems would collapse. Their movement and vitality would be lost.
That is why Osho’s thought remains a mystical idea rather than a practical reality.
articles.longDescription:
Freedom and Faith: The Sweet Illusion That Sustains Us


Osho once said that no one truly wants to take responsibility; everyone simply wants freedom. If that were completely true, the systems we see today—let alone Osho’s own commune—would never have existed. Society functions and progresses only because there are enough people, in every sphere from family to government, who are willing to sacrifice their personal freedom and endure hardship. If every individual were to become absolutely free, all existing systems would collapse. Their movement and vitality would be lost. That is why Osho’s thought remains a mystical idea rather than a practical reality.


Rabindranath Tagore, in his immortal Gitanjali, expresses a journey of spiritual evolution. He first declares, I do not want to be a believer; I want to be knowledgeable. Then he rises to an even higher stage: I do not want to be knowledgeable; I want to be so innocent that existence itself reveals its secrets to me. This too is a mystical thought. The greatest challenge for a human being is to be pure—free from the clutter of desires. Tagore knew well that purity is impossible if one remains entangled in endless wants. He refused to be worshipped as a saint because he believed that purity is not the privilege of a few; it is inherent in all creation. God resides in every human being, in the clouds, the trees, and the ocean. If God is everywhere, whom should we worship? This is the question Tagore asks, and it is a question each of us must ask ourselves.


Man constantly yearns for freedom but resists it at the same time. He longs to break his chains, yet clings to them because, paradoxically, they give comfort and joy. Freedom can seem frightening, unsafe, and unprotected. Why should one voluntarily walk toward uncertainty when the known offers warmth and security? Even saints and spiritual seekers, who speak of surrendering everything to reach God’s feet, often hesitate to renounce the comforts of power, wealth, or recognition. The warriors of history—those who fought for their country’s freedom or for lofty ideals—are exceptions. They broke the roots of comfort and took flight, often sacrificing their lives. Their minds, fixed on a higher goal, were arguably freer than those of monks giving spiritual sermons. Their death itself became a declaration of freedom.


Yet complete freedom remains, in many ways, an illusion. True freedom demands giving up all comforts, even life itself. Spiritual teachers may call this the highest liberation, but the fear of hunger, thirst, and death pulls most people back from such a path. Only a rare few overcome this fear and rise to that priceless freedom. Even Tagore, who dedicated himself to the universe through Gitanjali, could not fully achieve it in real life.


The ancient theory that everything is an illusion still rings true. Consider lovers locked in a room without basic amenities. At first, their passion may seem unshakable. But after days of hunger, sweat, and bodily discomfort, disgust will replace desire. The body’s realities strip love of its romantic glow, revealing that lust, beauty, and even affection are sustained more by the mind than by the flesh. Similarly, imagine a family stranded at sea without food or water. In the fight for survival, love and tenderness would quickly give way to suspicion and fear. Compassion would crumble under the weight of primal instinct. What we call love or nobility is often a delicate illusion—sweet but fragile. Perhaps it is better for a person not to shatter these illusions, but instead to recognize that the prison of comforting dreams is sometimes sweeter than the harshness of absolute freedom.


Man is a being of split personality. Within him, countless ideas and conflicting thoughts are born every moment. They battle each other, and whichever is stronger wins—whether for good or ill. This inner conflict is shaped by genetics, chemical reactions in the body, and the state of the mind at any given instant. He is never fully in control.


Man’s search for God is equally complex. He travels to temples, mosques, and churches, finding joy in the search itself. That joy lies partly in the fact that God can never be directly seen; if he could, the quest would end—and with it, the thrill of seeking. Although sages teach that God ultimately resides within, common sense often resists this truth. That is why reformers like Sree Narayana Guru built temples for the common people and gave them a simple principle:When you think and act well, you see God; when you think and act badly, you see the devil. Every human being is a seeker of truth, yet the truth is elusive and differs from person to person, from subject to subject. What, then, is the ultimate truth? It cannot be captured by any man-made system, for all such systems are imperfect. Perhaps truth itself is God.


In the face of such imperfection, only honesty offers a glimmer of light. If one lives truthfully, one need not be devotee of any cult. It is enough to be a person of sincerity, compassion, love, and humanity. But because this path is difficult, most people choose the easier way: belief in God. Faith provides comfort and peace of mind, allowing life to move forward with hope and meaning. Let that faith continue.

articles.title: Freedom – Part Seven
articles.shortDescription: Is freedom about standing outside society? Is it about avoiding everything, not reacting to anything, and living as if nothing around us matters? Such a life of detachment is one of indifference. But human birth is not meant for detachment; it is meant for attachment. A person without attachment to life finds no meaning in it. Such a birth, steeped in detachment, would itself seem like a mistake.
articles.longDescription:
Society and the Struggle Against Change

Is freedom about standing outside society? Is it about avoiding everything, not reacting to anything, and living as if nothing around us matters? Such a life of detachment is one of indifference. But human birth is not meant for detachment; it is meant for attachment. A person without attachment to life finds no meaning in it. Such a birth, steeped in detachment, would itself seem like a mistake.


Many philosophers claim that freedom means understanding oneself. But what exactly should one understand within a single lifetime? Osho says that to free the soul without injuries, one must understand the game of life and break its chains. Yet it is ironic that such ideas are often put forward by modern-day ascetics who live at the height of material comfort, surrounded by disciples and luxury. There is a vast gap between their discourse and their lived reality. They tell us to save the soul, but the truth is: when the body stops, the soul will naturally move on without anyone’s help.


The real way to preserve the soul is to live as a human being—with love, tenderness, and compassion. Spread happiness. Learn to forgive and forget, and refuse to become a slave to love and hate. Ordinary people may find this nearly impossible, but that state is the essence of ultimate happiness. To reach it is to find true freedom.


It is true that man is born imperfect. But through many stages of growth, he evolves. This is both the pain and the joy of human birth. Life is like a seed growing into a sapling, then into a tree that enjoys many seasons—flowering, shedding leaves, sprouting again. Unlike animals, who attain maturity quickly and live within fixed boundaries, man grows slowly, both physically and mentally. While the body eventually stops growing, the mind continues to evolve every day. Human life is therefore vertical—an upward journey. Only in old age does one descend the mountain, with the body and mind weakening. Yet even then, the soul—his true energy—remains untouched.


A seeker of truth must be able to absorb what is right, think freely, and act creatively. Such assimilation leads to freedom, and freedom in turn leads to creativity. That is when a person truly sees, hears, and experiences the universe. Yet not everyone reaches this stage—and that is the very beauty of life.


Humans also inherit a unique power: the accumulated knowledge and experience of generations. Unlike animals, humans carry within their DNA the wisdom of thousands of years—social, cultural, economic, and spiritual. A child quickly adapts to technology because a reservoir of knowledge already exists within. Intelligence, strength, and artistic ability also flow through generations.


The duty of every human being is to build upon that inheritance and move forward. True freedom is achieved when one recognizes and uses this great heritage—not merely for oneself, but for future generations. Otherwise, people remain prisoners of the past, bound by its memories. Lost opportunities of inquiry and progress must then be painfully rediscovered by those who come later. If ignored, society begins to regress.


The journey of life must eventually lead to peace. If one can face the final days without clinging to wealth, property, family, health, or the fear of death, then he dies as a free person. But how many people achieve that? Very few. Most die still bound by desires and worries. In this, there is little difference between ordinary people and so-called great souls. Perhaps some ascetics who renounce everything might reach liberation—but even that is uncertain.


The vast majority of people live by compromise. Those who accept this limited freedom enjoy a relatively comfortable life; those who resist it suffer. Most people also lean toward conservatism, rejecting anything that threatens their comfort. They oppose new ideas, resist revolutions, and fear change—whether great or small. Such people once opposed Socrates, Christ, Muhammad, and Buddha. They persecuted anyone who challenged superstition and authority.


But history shows that it is not the majority who transform society—it is always individuals. Independent thinkers who dare to question the system. The universe entrusts them with this task. Free from many chains, they challenge existing laws, customs, and beliefs. Their mantra is simple: change. They dream great dreams—many of which seem impossible. The masses call them mad. Yet what begins as madness often becomes tomorrow’s reality.


Society that clings only to the past can never progress. The law of the universe is that the old must die for the new to be born. Those who fight for change are not afraid of loss. They break laws, defy customs, and even sacrifice their lives for a greater tomorrow. This is the mark of true freedom.

articles.shortDescription: Love and hate are the two fundamental emotions of human life. Can one truly live without hating anyone or anything, while loving everyone and everything? It sounds like an impossible commandment. It is not easy to love everyone and everything. Such boundless love and the absence of hatred can exist only in a truly free person.
articles.longDescription:
The Liberation of the Heart

Love and hate are the two fundamental emotions of human life. Can one truly live without hating anyone or anything, while loving everyone and everything? It sounds like an impossible commandment. It is not easy to love everyone and everything. Such boundless love and the absence of hatred can exist only in a truly free person.


Ordinary people experience love in varying degrees—intense love, affection, or indifference. Hatred too has its own gradations. Yet, love itself brings sorrow. The absence of love, the feeling of being unloved, or the loss of a loved one—all cause pain.


The depth of hatred is often greater than the depth of love. Therefore, the elimination of hatred is the real path to freedom. Freedom from hatred removes the negative energy within us and fills the mind and body with vitality. That is the true state of love—not the love for a partner, but the love one feels for one’s own being, the environment, nature, or dreams.


If the mind is filled with hatred, one begins to hate oneself, the surroundings, the body, the universe, and even one’s dreams. This should never happen. When life becomes boundless love, there are no big or small feelings towards anyone. There are no demands, superiority, or expectations. When these vanish, disappointment disappears too.


Sadness arises when love is measured—when we feel its weight or length has diminished. This measurement breeds hatred. In essence, problems arise from expecting too much from others. No matter how close a person is, expect nothing from them. Spread love without expectation—then hatred will disappear.


It is not easy to live without being entangled in relationships. Hence, it is natural for human beings to experience love and hate in varying proportions. The average life is a struggle for existence, and that struggle continues for all living beings until they die. Life is not eternal. We should be able to look at this transient life with compassion, not greed. The essential element for that is love—a divine gift of nature. It should be preserved and enjoyed without losing it.


Karl Marx viewed marriage as an absurd institution. But without marriage, there is no family; without family, there is no nation; and without these two, there is no love. The Russian government understood this and therefore did not reject the family system. Osho too followed Marx, advocating a world without marriage, family, or countries—one world where people roam freely. Osho calls this heaven. But would it truly be heaven—or chaos?


A so-called free man, governed only by ego, will display all his pride. Both Osho and Marx seem to forget that the basic instinct of man is to capture and conquer. In such a free society, women would suffer the most. How many free men would be capable of noble, spiritual love? Lust would rule the majority, creating chaos and fear—and love would die.


Action is a joy, but reaction need not be. If praise brings joy, criticism often brings anger and hatred. This is an unseen slavery. When action brings pleasure, reaction brings bondage. Whether the reaction is good or bad, the only way to remain calm is not to listen to it. Listening to praise or criticism unconsciously binds us—it conditions the mind.


We must remember that every human being is conditioned in some way. Humility, restraint, silence, and endurance are all forms of conditioning. This conditioning begins in schools, homes, society, and workplaces. The difference between domesticated and wild animals illustrates this well—domesticated animals lose the freedom nature gave them. Likewise, humans remain conditioned from birth to death. Lack of freedom has become man’s defining trait—a genetic condition passed through generations.


Yet, this conditioning has its utility. If man were allowed to achieve everything he desired, his life would be short-lived, for every system would work against him.


Osho said that the suppression of desire is the greatest tragedy of mankind, and that patience, love, and non-violence cultivated through training are forms of hypocrisy. But such ideas can only lead to an anarchic society. Freedom does not mean permission to do whatever one likes. True freedom and joy lie somewhere between restriction and permission—a balance as serene as the silence of the Buddha.


This balance may not always bring personal happiness, but it aligns with what society expects of us. Thus arises a profound question: Whose happiness do we live for? A selfless life means that our happiness becomes part of society’s happiness. That is what makes life meaningful. A life of total selfishness can never be truly happy—unless one is completely withdrawn from the world.


The truth is, there is more than one person within each of us. They often quarrel with each other. When two such personalities marry, the conflict intensifies. When children and relatives join, it becomes a riot. When this enters the social system, it becomes a tragedy. Perhaps this is why the Bible says that man is born a sinner and dies a sinner.


This also explains why power and wealth in the world often end up in the wrong hands. But awareness of this truth helps preserve self-respect. One can then love people despite their flaws. This love does not mean blindly trusting religious, community, or political leaders, for they often sow the seeds of hatred. True freedom from hatred comes from understanding what is right and wrong in their words and acting accordingly.


Society needs more people who can love others without greed, ambition, or ego. When such people increase, an awakening will occur in a decaying society. Even if they cannot change the world, they can love it and enjoy life deeply.


Use this precious opportunity of life to celebrate, not to fight or hate. This doesn’t mean retreating to the mountains. Live within society—but without greed, ambition, or hatred. Love others, desire no one’s love in return. Then you can truly enjoy and celebrate life.


A person who transforms himself in this way becomes a source of inspiration to others. His change spreads silently. His presence radiates peace and love. That is where unconditional love becomes truly powerful.


It is sadness that must be eliminated. Make life joyful by adding something new every day. The political games of rulers, the voices of hatred from religious leaders, and even personal or natural tragedies—none of these should disturb your peace. That is true freedom, and that freedom is rebellion.


Rulers commit evils, and when the opposition comes to power, they repeat the same. They silence those who challenge them. If we can understand this truth, sorrow itself will change for the better. Another cause of sorrow is living trapped in the past. Every day should be a lesson in moving forward without looking back.


May you be among those who leave behind the darkness of night and embrace the light of morning with love.

articles.shortDescription: Children typically grow up guided by adult advice. While this guidance is crucial for escaping immediate dangers, it can, at times, stifle the curiosity necessary to explore untraveled paths. Warnings—that one road is dangerous, another treacherous, and that only established routes should be followed—restrict the mind. An individual who internalizes these limits loses the desire to dive into the ocean or soar into the sky, remaining confined.
articles.longDescription:
The Birth of the Free Mind

Children typically grow up guided by adult advice. While this guidance is crucial for escaping immediate dangers, it can, at times, stifle the curiosity necessary to explore untraveled paths. Warnings—that one road is dangerous, another treacherous, and that only established routes should be followed—restrict the mind. An individual who internalizes these limits loses the desire to dive into the ocean or soar into the sky, remaining confined.


To overcome this limitation, intellectual freedom and free thinking must be cultivated. Education should be the catalyst for this growth. A teacher’s role is to reveal a world of limitless potential to the student, not one filled with barriers. True life begins when one confronts, with open eyes, the very things that cause fear. Everything else is merely a repetition of the past. A true spiritual birth occurs when we realize there is nothing in this world to fear. This awakening is not confined to childhood, adolescence, or youth; it can happen even in old age. This moment marks one's authentic birth—a moment when one's responsibilities also increase, because from then on, every thought, feeling, and action is truly one's own.


Reaching this state necessitates making mistakes, for mistakes are the crucible of maturity. However, someone who repeats the same errors is not yet ready for such purity. To unlock this freedom, each person must undertake a rigorous self-examination. The layers of accumulated conditioning must be cleansed, the rusty chains of habit cast off, and absolute intellectual freedom declared. Only then can one transcend the past and the future, dwelling fully in the present. In that present, one lives without the pain of past regrets or the anxiety of future worries.


Such a liberated life requires that laws and regulations remain open to change. Just as a constitution must be amended, religious codes must also evolve with time. We must recognize that religion is a human construct, and therefore must adapt as humanity changes. Conservative minds must accept this reality; otherwise, while science accelerates human progress, unexamined religious doctrine risks plunging mankind into darkness. Religion is not a subject to be passively taught; it is a profound area each individual must study and question for themselves. There is no greater intellectual blindness than accepting, without critical inquiry, the ideas and imaginations developed two or four millennia ago. Humanity must stand with truth, not merely with blind faith.


Every individual exists simultaneously as a social institution—a composite created by family and society—and as a soul, which exists beyond this external construction. This explains why humans sometimes behave mechanically, and at other times act according to their true nature. This is not a split personality; one is the performer, and the other is the genuine self. Confronting this reality sometimes frightens and sometimes amazes us, for humanity is a being of immense diversity.


The individual moulded by society is a manufactured being. They run endlessly—chasing money, power, prestige, and respect—constantly worrying about unfulfilled desires. These insatiable wants cling to them like a spiritual plague, persisting even as death approaches. From the moment of self-awareness, humanity begins to fear death. This fear quickly transforms into anxiety about what must be done before dying. People even perform rituals to appease the dead, hoping the next generation will offer them the same homage.


In short, no other creature on Earth is as intensely attached to life as humanity. This attachment has persisted, largely unchanged, since the dawn of primitive knowledge. Only when this bond is broken can an individual attain the freedom to live in accordance with their soul—to live with true and unburdened expression.


The great spiritual and intellectual figures throughout history trained themselves for this liberation. We, too, can achieve this transformation. Every human being who identifies and overcomes the social systems that attempt to reduce them to mere commodities and tools of survival joins that same lineage of the great—those who stood for truth, enacted social change, and accepted the resulting punishment for speaking their mind.

articles.shortDescription:
A visit to Palakkad for a friend’s daughter’s wedding became a lesson in the beauty of ordinary life.
A bus conductor stopped to collect drinking water from a public tap. A small tea-shop couple managed their work calmly even when their regular worker was absent.
A traditional chirava I bought for a friend brought us another small moment of friendship and humour.
At the wedding, old friends travelled from different places, filling the gathering with affection, laughter and memories. The convention centre also created livelihood opportunities for local women.
A conductor. A tea-shop couple. Women running small enterprises. Friends travelling long distances. A simple chirava bringing people together.
None of these is extraordinary. Yet they reveal something important:
Simplicity is not the absence of complexity. It is finding meaning and happiness in what is ordinary and necessary.
That was Palakkad’s message to me.
articles.title: Simple and Complex – Episode 4 Palakkad’s Simplicity: Small Things, Quiet Lives

പാലക്കാട് ഒരുക്കിയ ലാളിത്യം

എന്നോടൊപ്പം ഡൽഹി കേരള ഹൌസിൽ ജോലി ചെയ്തിരുന്ന ഹരിദാസിന്‍റെ മകളുടെ വിവാഹം കൂടാനായിരുന്നു ഇത്തവണത്തെ പാലക്കാട് യാത്ര.ഹോട്ടൽ നളന്ദ ഇന്നിലായിരുന്നു മുറി ബുക്ക് ചെയ്തിരുന്നത്.ഞാൻ കയറിയ ബസ് നളന്ദ കടന്ന് അൽപ്പം മുന്നോട്ടുപോയി നിന്നു.ട്രാഫിക്കാവും എന്നാണ് കരുതിയത്.നോക്കുമ്പോള്‍ കണ്ടക്ടർ വഴിയിൽ ഇറങ്ങി ടാപ്പിൽ നിന്നും വെള്ളം പിടിക്കുകയാണ്.ഞാൻ പതുക്കെ അവിടെയിറങ്ങി.പിറകോട്ടുനടന്ന് ഹോട്ടലിലെത്തി.റോഡിന്‍റെ ഒരു വശത്ത് നളന്ദ ഇന്നും മറുവശം നളന്ദ റിച്ചുമാണ്.എനിക്ക് മുറി റിച്ചിലായിരുന്നു.മുറിയെടുത്തശേഷം അവരുടെ റസ്റ്ററന്‍റിൽ വന്ന് ഭക്ഷണം കഴിച്ചു.കുറച്ചു സമയം വിശ്രമിച്ചശേഷം പുറത്തിറങ്ങി.നാലരയായി.വെറുതെ മുന്നോട്ടുനടന്നപ്പോള്‍ പാലക്കാട് കോട്ട കണ്ടു.പണ്ടൊരിക്കൽ അവിടെവന്നത് ഓർത്തു.അതിനോട് ചേർന്നുള്ള വാടിക ഗാർഡനിൽ ഇരുപത്തിയഞ്ച് രൂപ ടിക്കറ്റെടുത്ത് കയറി.കുട്ടികളുമായി വന്ന് സമയം ചിലവഴിക്കാൻ കൊള്ളാവുന്ന ഇടമാണ്.കുറച്ചുസമയം അവിടെ ചുറ്റി നടന്ന് പുറത്തിറങ്ങി.അപ്പോള്‍ അഞ്ചേകാലായി.കോട്ട അഞ്ചരയ്ക്ക് അടയ്ക്കും.അതിന്‍റെ പരിസരത്ത് കുറച്ചുസമയം ചിലവിട്ട് വീണ്ടും നടന്നു.വലതുവശത്തെ രക്തസാക്ഷി മണ്ഡപവുമൊക്കെ കണ്ട് തെരുവിലൂടെ വെറുതെ നടന്നു.ഡിസംബറിന്‍റെ രണ്ടാം പകുതിയാണ്.ആളുകള്‍ ക്രിസ്തുമസ്-പുതുവത്സര വിപണികളിൽ തിരക്കിലാണ്.പ്രത്യേകിച്ചൊന്നും വാങ്ങാനില്ലാത്തതിനാൽ അലയുക മാത്രമായിരുന്നു ലക്ഷ്യം.


തൃശൂരിലേക്ക് തിരിയുന്ന റോഡും ഒലവക്കോട് കോഴിക്കോട് റോഡുമുണ്ട്.കോഴിക്കോട് റോഡിലേക്ക് തിരിഞ്ഞു.നടത്തക്കിടയിൽ ടൌണ്‍ ബസ്സ്റ്റാൻഡിൽ എത്തി.അവിടെ നടത്തിയ അന്വേഷണത്തിൽ ഹരിദാസിന്‍റെ മകളുടെ വിവാഹത്തിന് എത്തേണ്ട പെരിങ്ങോട് ഇറങ്ങാൻ മുനിസിപ്പൽ സ്റ്റാൻഡിൽ നിന്നും ചെർപ്പുളശ്ശേരി ബസ് പിടിച്ചാൽ മതിയെന്ന് മനസിലാക്കി.രാവിലെ ആ വഴിക്കാവാം നീക്കം എന്നും നിശ്ചയിച്ചു.മധുരയിൽ നിന്നും സുഹൃത്ത് ഹരി ഇന്നലെ വിളിച്ച് ചിരവ വാങ്ങാൻ കിട്ടുമോ എന്ന് നോക്കാൻ പറഞ്ഞത് ഓർമ്മയിലുണ്ടായിരുന്നു.കഴിഞ്ഞ വടക്കു-കിഴക്കൻ പ്രദേശ യാത്രയിൽ ഗോഹട്ടിയിലെ ഞങ്ങളുടെ ആതിഥേയനും ഒരു ഹരിയായിരുന്നു.അദ്ദേഹത്തിന്‍റെ വീട്ടിലാണ് പരന്ന പ്രതലമുള്ള സ്ലാബിൽ വച്ച് തേങ്ങ ചിരവാന്‍ പറ്റുന്ന ഉപകരണം ഹരി കണ്ടത്.അതിൽ ആകൃഷ്ടനായ അദ്ദേഹം അന്നുമുതൽ അതിന് പിന്നാലെയാണ്.കോയമ്പത്തൂരാണ് അത് നിർമ്മിക്കുന്നത്,അവിടെ നോക്കണം എന്നു പറയാനാണ് ഇന്നലെ വിളിച്ചത്.നിർമ്മിക്കുന്നിടത്തെ കടകളിൽ ഇതുണ്ടാകാൻ സാധ്യത കുറവാകുമെന്ന് ഞാൻ ചിന്തിച്ചു.കാരണം ചിരവ കൂടുതലായി ഉപയോഗിക്കുന്നത് മലയാളിയാണ്,അതുകൊണ്ട് തമിഴ്നാട്ടിൽ ഇതിന് വിൽപ്പന കുറവാകും.കോയമ്പത്തൂരിലെ മെഷീൻ നിർമ്മാതാക്കള്‍ വലിയ വിദഗ്ധരാണ്.ഏത് ആശയം കൊണ്ടുവന്നു കൊടുത്താലും അവർ അതിനനുസരണമായ ഉപകരണമുണ്ടാക്കും.അത്തരത്തിലാകും പുതിയ ചിരവയും ജന്മമെടുത്തത്.പാലക്കാടുള്ള കടകളിൽ ഇതുണ്ടാകും എന്ന കണക്ക് തെറ്റിയില്ല.ഒരു കടയുടെ മുന്നിൽ ചിരവ കാണുകയും രണ്ടെണ്ണം വാങ്ങുകയും ചെയ്തു.ഒന്ന് പച്ച പെയിന്‍റ് അടിച്ചതും മറ്റൊന്ന് സ്റ്റീലും.തിരിച്ച് മുറിയിലെത്തി അതിന്‍റെ ചിത്രം ഹരിക്ക് അയച്ചുകൊടുത്തു.അപ്പോള്‍ പെയിന്‍റടിച്ച ചിരവ വേണ്ട,സ്റ്റീൽ നിറമുള്ളത് മതി എന്നായി.അത് കൊടുക്കാം എന്ന് ഞാനും പറഞ്ഞു.പാലക്കാട് വിവാഹത്തിൽ പങ്കെടുക്കാനായി രാത്രിയിൽ ടൌണ്‍ റയിൽവേ സ്റ്റേഷനിലിറങ്ങിയ ഹരി നേരെ ഹോട്ടലിലെത്തി.ഞങ്ങള്‍ ഒന്നിച്ച് അത്താഴം കഴിച്ചു.സ്റ്റീൽ ചിരവയുമായി അദ്ദേഹം ഒലവക്കോട് റയിൽവേ സ്റ്റേഷനിൽ ബുക്ക് ചെയ്തിരിക്കുന്ന താമസസ്ഥലത്തേക്ക് പോയി.


രാവിലെ ഒരു ആട്ടോയിൽ മുനിസിപ്പൽ ബസ്റ്റാന്‍റിലെത്തി.അവിടെനിന്നും ചെർപ്പുളശ്ശേരി ബസിൽ കയറി.ഒലവക്കോട് സ്റ്റേഷനിൽ നിന്നും ഹരിയും കയറി.ഞങ്ങള്‍ നേരത്തെതന്നെ കല്യാണസ്ഥലത്തെത്തി.അവിടെയുള്ള ചായക്കടയിൽ നിന്നും ഇഡ്ഡലി കഴിച്ചു.ദമ്പതിമാർ ചേർന്നാണ് കട നടത്തുന്നത്.അവർ കൃത്യമായ ഒരു റിഥത്തിൽ പൂരിയും ഇഡ്ഡലിയും ദോശയും ചപ്പാത്തിയുമൊക്കെ ഉണ്ടാക്കുകയും വിളമ്പുകയും ചെയ്യുന്നത് കാണാൻ ഒരു ചന്തമുണ്ടായിരുന്നു.അത് പറഞ്ഞപ്പോഴാണ് കടയുടമ ജോലിക്കാരൻ ഇന്ന് വന്നിട്ടില്ല എന്ന് പറഞ്ഞത്.അതിന്‍റെ കുറവ് അറിയിക്കാതെയും ആശങ്കകള്‍ ഇല്ലാതെയുമാണ് അവർ കച്ചവടം നടത്തിവന്നത്.


അവിടെനിന്നും നടന്ന് ഞങ്ങള്‍ ഫൈവ് ക്ലൌഡ് കണ്‍വെൻഷൻ സെന്‍ററിലെത്തി.അവിടെ സ്ത്രീകള്‍ ക്ലീനിംഗ് ജോലി ചെയ്യുന്നു.ഹരിദാസിന്‍റെ ബന്ധുക്കള്‍ ചിലർ വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്.തൊട്ടടുത്ത് ഒരു ക്ഷേത്രം കണ്ടു.പ്രധാന റോഡിൽ നിന്നും കുറച്ച് അകത്താണ്.ഞങ്ങള്‍ അവിടേക്ക് പോയി.ശരീരി ശ്രീ ദുർഗ്ഗാ ക്ഷേത്രത്തിൽ പോറ്റിയും രണ്ട് സ്ത്രീകളുമുണ്ടായിരുന്നു.അധികമാളുകള്‍ വരുന്ന ഇടമല്ല എന്നുതോന്നി.നാട്ടിൻപുറത്തിന്‍റെ ശാലീനതയുള്ള ക്ഷേത്രത്തിൽ ഉടുപ്പൂരി കയറേണ്ടതിനാൽ ഞാൻ കയറിയില്ല.ഹരി കയറുകയും പൂജയ്ക്ക് പണം നൽകുകയും ചെയ്തു.ഞങ്ങള്‍ തിരികെ എത്തിയപ്പോഴേക്കും ഹരിദാസും ചന്ദ്രികയുമൊക്കെ ഹാളിൽ എത്തിയിരുന്നു.കല്യാണമണ്ഡപത്തിന്‍റെ മാനേജരെ പരിചയപ്പെട്ടു.അദ്ദേഹം ഇരുപത്തിനാല് മണിക്കൂറും അതിന്‍റെ ചുമതലക്കാരനാണ്.കണ്‍വെൻഷൻ സെന്‍ററിന്‍റെ ഉടമകള്‍ മൂന്ന് പേരാണ്.അവരുടെ പ്രധാന ബിസിനസ് ടയർ വ്യാപാരമാണ്.കണ്‍വെൻഷൻ സെന്‍ററിന് നല്ല പാർക്കിംഗ് ഏരിയയും അകത്ത് രണ്ടായിരം പേർക്കിരിക്കാവുന്ന സൌകര്യവും നല്ല സ്റ്റേജും ഊണിടവുമുണ്ട്.അതിന് പിന്നിൽ താമസസൌകര്യവുമുണ്ട്.ഡൽഹി കേരള ഹൌസിൽ ഞങ്ങള്‍ക്കൊപ്പം ജോലി ചെയ്തിരുന്ന ശ്രീദേവനും ശുഭയും അവിടെയാണ് താമസിക്കുന്നത്.പത്തനംതിട്ടയിൽ നിന്നും ശിവദാസനും ഭാര്യയും എത്തിയിട്ടുണ്ടായിരുന്നു.അവർ വെളുപ്പിന് രണ്ടു മണിക്ക് കാറിൽ പുറപ്പെട്ട് പാലക്കാട് എത്തിയതാണ്.അവരുമായി വിശേഷം പങ്കിടുമ്പോള്‍ ഹരിദാസും ചന്ദ്രികയും വന്നു.സന്തോഷവർത്തമാനങ്ങള്‍ക്കിടയിൽ തിരുവനന്തപുരത്തുനിന്നും മറ്റിടങ്ങളിൽ നിന്നുമുള്ള സുഹൃത്തുക്കളും പങ്കുചേർന്നു.ഗോപൻ,ഷാജി,അനില,കൃഷ്ണചന്ദ്രൻ,സുരേന്ദ്രൻ,ഭാര്യ,കുട്ടനും രാജിയും,സരസമ്മ,രജനി,ഭർത്താവ്,മകള്‍,ഗോവിന്ദരാജ്,എ.ആർ.രാജു,ഭാര്യ,ദയകുമാർ,ശ്രീജിത്ത്,മോഹനൻ,ശൈലേഷ് തുടങ്ങി ഒരുവലിയ നിരതന്നെ വന്നുചേർന്നു.എല്ലാവരും പരസ്പ്പരം സ്നേഹം പങ്കിട്ടു.ഇതിനിടയിൽ വിവാഹചടങ്ങുകള്‍ ആരംഭിച്ചു.വരനെ സ്വീകരിക്കലും കല്യാണവും.വലിയ സ്റ്റേജും ഫോട്ടോഗ്രാഫർമാർക്ക് താഴെനിന്ന് നന്നായി ചിത്രമെടുക്കാനുള്ള സൌകര്യവും ഒരുക്കിയിട്ടും വിവാഹത്തെ ബന്ധുക്കളും ഫോട്ടോഗ്രാഫർമാരും കൂടി മനുഷ്യമതിൽകെട്ടി മറച്ചതിനാൽ സദസിലിരുന്ന ഭൂരിപക്ഷത്തിന് വിവാഹം കാണാൻ കഴിഞ്ഞില്ല.ദക്ഷിണകേരളത്തിലെ സദ്യപോലെ ആയിരുന്നില്ലെങ്കിലും നല്ല സദ്യയായിരുന്നു സ്ത്രീകൂട്ടായ്മ ഒരുക്കിയത്.പ്രദേശത്തെ സ്ത്രീകള്‍ക്ക് ഉപജീവനത്തിന് ബലം പകരുന്ന സംരംഭമാണ് ഫൈവ് ക്ലൌഡ് എന്നും മനസിലാക്കി.

articles.title: Thirteen Years, 527 Pages—and Still No Final Justice
articles.shortDescription:
The Tarun Tejpal case began in 2013. The trial started in 2017, the Sessions Court delivered a 527-page judgment in 2021, and the Bombay High Court has now reversed that verdict and sentenced Tejpal to ten years’ rigorous imprisonment.

The matter is still not over. The Supreme Court remains the next stage.

Whatever the final judicial outcome may be, one question cannot be ignored:

Can a justice system that takes thirteen years to reach this stage be called an effective system of justice?

Fair trial, due process and protection of the rights of both the accused and the survivor are essential. But justice must also be timely.

When litigation consumes years of people’s lives, enormous resources and emotional energy, delay itself becomes a form of suffering.

The purpose of courts is not merely to produce lengthy judgments. It is to deliver justice—fairly, efficiently and within a reasonable time.

Thirteen years. 527 pages. And the case is still not over.

Is this justice?

“Reforming the judiciary is not weakening the judiciary. It is strengthening justice.”
articles.longDescription:
പതിമൂന്ന് വർഷം,527 പേജ് – ഇതോ നീതി?

ഒളിക്യാമറ വച്ച് സെൻസേഷണൽ വാർത്തകളുണ്ടാക്കി കുപ്രസിദ്ധി നേടിയ തെഹൽക മാസികയുടെ മുൻ പത്രാധിപർ തരുണ്‍ തേജ്പാലിനെ സഹപ്രവർത്തകയെ ബലാത്സംഗം ചെയ്തെന്ന കേസ്സിൽ ബോംബെ ഹൈക്കോടതി പത്തു വർഷം കഠിനതടവിന് ശിക്ഷിച്ചു.യുവതിക്ക് പത്ത് ലക്ഷം രൂപ നഷ്ടപരിഹാരം നൽകണമെന്നും വിധിയിൽ പറയുന്നു.2013 ലാണ് ആരോപിത സംഭവം നടന്നത്.ഗോവയിൽ തെഹൽക നടത്തിയ തിങ്ക് ഫെസ്റ്റിനിടെ ലിഫ്റ്റിൽ വച്ച് ലൈംഗികമായി ഉപദ്രവിച്ചു എന്നായിരുന്നു കേസ്.2013 നവംബർ 20 ന് തരുണ്‍ എഡിറ്റർ സ്ഥാനം രാജിവച്ചു.നവംബർ 30 ന് മുൻകൂർ ജാമ്യം കിട്ടാതെ കീഴടങ്ങി.2014 ഫെബ്രുവരിയിൽ കുറ്റപത്രം സമർപ്പിച്ചു.2014 ജൂലൈ ഒന്നിന് സുപ്രിംകോടതി ജാമ്യം അനുവദിച്ചു.2017 സെപ്തംബറിൽ വിചാരണ തുടങ്ങി.2021 മെയ് 21 ന് കേസ് തെളിയിക്കാൻ പ്രോസിക്യൂഷന് കഴിഞ്ഞില്ല എന്ന് 527 പേജുള്ള വിധിന്യായത്തിൽ സെഷൻസ് കോടതി ജഡ്ജി പ്രഖ്യാപിച്ചു.തുടർന്ന് ഹൈക്കോടതിയിലെത്തിയ കേസ്സിലാണ് 2026 ഓഗസ്റ്റ് 6ന് ശിക്ഷ വിധിച്ചത്.തുടർന്നുള്ള അങ്കം സുപ്രിം കോടതിയിലാണ്.അവിടെയെന്താകും നിലപാട് എന്നറിയില്ല?


ഇവിടെ പ്രസക്തമാകുന്നത് ഇത്രയുമാണ്.ലിഫ്റ്റിൽ വച്ച് തന്നെ ഉപദ്രവിച്ചു എന്ന് ഒരു സ്ത്രീ ആരോപണം നടത്തിയത് അന്വേഷിച്ച് വിധി പറയാനെടുത്തത് പതിമൂന്ന് വർഷം.കുറ്റാരോപിതനെ വെറുതെവിട്ട കോടതി തയ്യാറാക്കിയ വിധി പ്രസ്താവത്തിന് 527 പേജ്.കേസ്സ് അവസാനിക്കുന്നില്ല.ഇവിടെ ആരോപിതനും അതിജീവിതയും അവരുടെ ജീവിതത്തിന്‍റെ നല്ല പങ്കും വലിയ തുകയും കേസ്സിനായി ചിലവഴിക്കുന്നു.സങ്കീർണ്ണമല്ലാത്ത ഒരു നീതി വ്യവസ്ഥയിൽ ഏറിയാൽ ഒരു മാസം കൊണ്ട് തീർപ്പാക്കാവുന്ന ഒരു കേസ്സ്. രാജഭരണത്തിലൊക്കെ ഒരു ദിവസം കൊണ്ട് തീർപ്പുണ്ടായേനെ. അതിലെ ശരി തെറ്റുകള്‍ എന്ത് എന്നറിയാൻ കഴിയില്ലെങ്കിലും അനിശ്ചിതമായി നീളുന്ന കേസ്സുകള്‍ മരണാസന്നനായി മരിക്കാതെ കിടക്കുന്ന ഒരു രോഗിയെ ഓർമ്മിപ്പിക്കുന്നു എന്നേ പറയാൻ കഴിയൂ. ഇന്ത്യൻ സംവിധാനത്തിൽ ഒരു മികച്ച നീതിന്യായ രീതി എന്നെങ്കിലും ഉണ്ടാകുമോ?
